The brazing process requires 600°C to 1000°C temperatures sustained for more than 1 hour, which significantly alters the copper microstructure. The electron beam process limits alteration of microstructure to within millimeters of the joint centerline and maintains a consistent chemistry with no use of braze alloy. Brazing often depends on capillary forces controlled by geometry and surface conditions for the braze alloy to flow and fill a joint. In contrast electron beam welding requires tight geometric tolerances but advanced control such as beam oscillation can accommodate joint fit-up issues. B.3.2 Equipment Considerations Internal vs External Electron Beam Gun There are two major configurations of electron beam guns: internally mounted on a motion control system (Figure 17), and externally mounted in a fixed position (Figure 18). The internal gun is limited to low voltage but the external gun can be either low or high accelerating voltage. The internal gun is also limited in size, whereas the external gun has no limit to column length. The longer column length enables integration of more focusing lenses and advanced electro-optical controls for beam manipulation. The smaller size of the internal gun also limits the additional vacuum that can be added to the column thus increasing its risk for contamination of the gun which can lead to defects in the welds. The major benefit of the internal gun is related to joint access on large assemblies without repositioning of the workpiece and inside of a smaller chamber compared to an external gun. This major benefit is why internal guns are often used for welding of large accelerator assemblies which have a series of joint types in a variety of positions. Internal guns often simplify fixturing and weld assembly design, particularly when it is possible to weld underneath the shadow of a flange using a tilt on the gun itself. High voltage systems can also generate greater net power with greater weld penetration. The smaller focus diameter is not necessarily beneficial for most joint types on copper accelerators, unless an advanced beam manipulation is used. The longer focal distance has three major benefits: longer depth of focus which increases the allowable position tolerance, joint access, and reduced contamination from materials vaporizing off the weld pool.
